newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Analysts say HK's Cathay Pacific forecasts unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say HK's Cathay Pacific forecasts unchanged.

text.p: Analysts said on Friday they were delaying revising formal profit forecasts for Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd until they know how long its fleet of Airbus A330-300 planes will be grounded with engine trouble.
"I haven't officially revised my forecasts downwards simply because of the fact that no one knows, even the management, what the actual impact is going to be," said K.Y. Ng of BZW Asia.
"We need to know, first of all, how long the planes will be grounded, (and) secondly, how much compensation they will receive from Rolls-Royce."
Cathay Pacific reported net profit of HK$3.81 billion (US$490 million) for the year to December 31, 1996, a 27.9 percent surge over 1995.
The consensus forecast for the 1997 year, as provided by Edinburgh Financial Publishing's The Estimate Directory, is net profit of HK$4.14 billion.

Cathay Pacific grounded all 11 of its Airbus A330-300s and Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd (Dragonair) -- 25.5 percent-owned by Cathay Pacific -- suspended four last Saturday after a series of single-engine landings due to problems with Rolls-Royce Plc Trent 700 engines.
Rolls-Royce said it had a solution to the problem, which stems from the lubrication system used in the Trent 700 gearbox.
The groundings have forced Cathay Pacific and Dragonair to cancel flights and charter aircraft to make up the shortfall.

Ng said until he had a clearer indication of how much compensation Cathay Pacific would get from Rolls-Royce, he would not revise a "guesstimate" the groundings would slice HK$200 million to HK$300 million from the airline's 1997 net profit.

An analyst with a Japanese institution said he would stick with his estimate the groundings would trim HK$100 million to HK$200 million from Cathay Pacific's net profits, based on a suspension period of three weeks.
New Rolls-Royce parts were coming in over the weekend to be fitted, Charlie Stewart-Cox, Cathay Pacific's general manager of group public affairs, told Reuters on Friday.
"It's feasible that an aircraft may get airborne even as early as Sunday," he said.
Depending on how the repairs went, it was possible all of Cathay Pacific's Airbus 330-300s could be airborne by "early in the second week of June", he said.
Analysts praised the speed with which Cathay Pacific had tackled the glitches with the engine.
"The problem is quite a large problem with the engines and they have done their best to cause minimum inconvenience to their customers," Ng said.
"They have been quite efficient in handling the problem," said the analyst with the Japanese institution. "The pace of progress has actually been faster than expected."
Cathay Pacific played down a newspaper report on Friday which said the airline had experienced shutdowns with Rolls-Royce RB211-524H engines on some Boeing 747 planes.
"There is nothing that indicates any cause of concern," Stewart-Cox said. "There is no trend that demonstrates any increasing rate of occurrence."
He said engine shutdowns occasionally happened in flight, often as a precautionary measure, and that the average number of shutdowns in the past year was in line with expectations.
Where shutdowns were outside normal levels, as with the Rolls-Royce Trent 700s on the Airbus A330-300s, additional checks were put in place, he said.
"There is no such issue with the RB-21s on the 747s," Stewart-Cox said.
